name: Beautiful Rectangle
description: You are given $$$n$$$ integers. You need to choose a subset and put the chosen numbers in a beautiful rectangle (rectangular matrix). Each chosen number should occupy one of its rectangle cells, each cell must be filled with exactly one chosen number. Some of the $$$n$$$ numbers may not be chosen. A rectangle (rectangular matrix) is called beautiful if in each row and in each column all values are different. What is the largest (by the total number of cells) beautiful rectangle you can construct? Print the rectangle itself.
input_specification: The first line contains $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 4\cdot10^5$$$). The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers ($$$1 \le a_i \le 10^9$$$).
output_specification: In the first line print $$$x$$$ ($$$1 \le x \le n$$$) — the total number of cells of the required maximum beautiful rectangle. In the second line print $$$p$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$p \cdot q=x$$$): its sizes. In the next $$$p$$$ lines print the required rectangle itself. If there are several answers, print any.
approach_summary: Precompute factorials and inverse factorials up to N using Fermat's Little Theorem (mod 10^9+7 or 998244353). Answer nCr queries in O(1) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1276C — Beautiful Rectangle [310. Large Factorials and Binomial Coefficients]
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Combinatorial selection $\binom{N}{K} = \frac{N!}{K!(N-K)!} \pmod P$ can be evaluated in $O(1)$ by precomputing factorials $fact[i] = fact[i-1] \cdot i \pmod P$ and inverse factorials $invFact[i] = invFact[i+1] \cdot (i+1) \pmod P$ using Fermat's Little Theorem $a^{P-2} \equiv a^{-1} \pmod P$.
